title: Broadcom Just Beat Every Estimate. Its Stock Fell 15 Per Cent Anyway. Here Is What NRI Investors Need to Understand.
excerpt: Record revenue, record margins, record AI bookings — and the worst single-day drop in months. The AI trade is entering a new phase where perfection is not enough.
body:
Broadcom reported its fiscal second-quarter earnings on Wednesday evening, and by every conventional measure, the numbers were spectacular. Revenue hit a record $22.2 billion, up 48 per cent year-over-year. AI semiconductor revenue reached $10.8 billion, a 143 per cent surge. Operating margins came in at 67 per cent. Free cash flow was $10.26 billion. Every number beat Wall Street estimates.

The stock dropped more than 15 per cent on Thursday.

If you own Broadcom — or any AI-adjacent name in your portfolio — this is the moment to understand what just changed.

## The Numbers Were Not the Problem

Broadcom's Q2 results were objectively strong. The company earned $2.44 per share on a non-GAAP basis, beating the consensus estimate of $2.40. Revenue of $22.19 billion topped the $21.71 billion analysts expected. Semiconductor solutions revenue alone was $15 billion — as much as the entire company generated in the same quarter a year ago.

CEO Hock Tan went further on the earnings call. AI semiconductor bookings during the quarter exceeded $30 billion — nearly three times what the company actually shipped. Tan guided Q3 AI semiconductor revenue to $16 billion, up over 200 per cent year-over-year. He reiterated the company's full-year AI semiconductor target of $56 billion and maintained the fiscal 2027 guidance of over $100 billion.

The guidance was not vague aspiration. Broadcom named its six core AI customers — including Alphabet, Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI — and described multi-generational chip development agreements extending into fiscal 2028.

## So Why Did It Fall?

The answer lies in the gap between what Broadcom delivered and what the market had already priced in. At its pre-earnings valuation of roughly $2.3 trillion, Broadcom was trading at levels that assumed not just strong execution, but perfection sustained over multiple years.

When every metric beats estimates and the stock still drops, it means expectations had moved beyond what any earnings report could satisfy. The market wanted not just a beat, but acceleration on a scale that even 143 per cent AI revenue growth could not deliver.

There is a structural issue compounding this. Broadcom's infrastructure software business — the VMware side of the house — grew just 9 per cent, contributing $7.17 billion. As AI hardware becomes a larger share of total revenue, the software segment's slower growth is dragging on the blended narrative. Margins in AI hardware are strong but structurally lower than software licensing, which creates mix-related margin pressure even as the business expands.

Analysts at Zacks noted that while the earnings beat was undeniable, management's framing was less about near-term outperformance and more about laying the groundwork for a multi-year AI infrastructure buildout — a timeline that patience-limited markets are less willing to pay for in advance.

## The AI Concentration Problem

Broadcom's fall did not happen in isolation. The broader chip sector pulled back, with the Nasdaq falling 1.2 per cent on Thursday as investors rotated out of high-momentum AI names. The S&P 500 broke a nine-day winning streak. Oil prices declined as Israel and Lebanon agreed to renew a ceasefire, slightly easing the geopolitical risk premium.

But the deeper issue is concentration. Broadcom acknowledged that its AI semiconductor growth is driven by six core customers. Alphabet alone accounts for a significant share through its TPU partnership. If any of these hyperscalers slows its capital expenditure — or shifts from custom ASICs to alternative architectures — Broadcom's growth trajectory would narrow considerably.

This is the same concentration risk that stalks the broader AI trade. The S&P 500 hit record highs earlier this week, but only two of its eleven sectors were positive on the day. AI and chip names are carrying the index while everything else lags. When those names stumble, as Broadcom did today, the impact ripples.

## What NRI Investors Should Know

For diaspora investors holding US-listed AI stocks — whether directly or through index funds — the Broadcom reaction carries three lessons.

First, valuations in AI infrastructure have moved past the point where beating estimates guarantees a positive stock reaction. The bar is not "good." The bar is "better than what the most optimistic institutional investor already modelled." That is an uncomfortable place to hold large positions.

Second, the memory chip shortage is real and ongoing. Morgan Stanley this week said there is "no quick fix" to the AI-driven memory shortage, and expects supply constraints to persist for two to three more years. Micron has nearly quadrupled in value this year. Sandisk is up 670 per cent. These are not speculative names — they are the infrastructure picks and shovels of the AI buildout — but their valuations now carry their own expectations burden.

Third, index fund investors are more exposed to AI concentration than they may realise. If you own the S&P 500 through a Vanguard or iShares fund, your portfolio is heavily weighted to a handful of AI-linked companies. A single bad day for Broadcom — a company that beat every estimate — cost the stock 15 per cent.

The AI infrastructure story is not over. Broadcom's fundamentals are genuinely strong, and the demand runway is long. But the market is now in a phase where strong is not strong enough. For NRI investors navigating this from abroad, the lesson is not to sell, but to understand that the rules of the AI trade have changed.

*Sources: Broadcom Q2 FY2026 earnings release and call transcript; Morgan Stanley equity research note on memory stocks; Investopedia market summary, June 4, 2026; Reuters market report*
